Lecture 21

Meromorphic functions, gamma continuation and residue sums

Lecture objectives

We prove that continuation along a path is unique, define meromorphic functions and show that a meromorphic continuation with poles in a suitable set is unique. A function already analytic on the plane minus its poles continues along every path without a choice, in contrast to the logarithm of Lecture 16. We prove that the gamma integral is analytic on the right half-plane, continue it to a meromorphic function on C,\CC, and compute the residues at its poles. Finally, we sum series over the integers with the auxiliary functions πcot⁡(πz)\pi\cot(\pi z)πcot(πz) and π/sin⁡(πz)\pi/\sin(\pi z)π/sin(πz) and explicit estimates on square paths.

Lecture 18 proved that an analytic function on a domain is determined by its values on any set with a limit point in the domain, and that an integral depending on a complex parameter is analytic under a domination condition. In this lecture we use both results to extend the gamma function of GM 27 from the positive real axis to the whole plane except the points 0,−1,−2,…,0,-1,-2,\ldots0,−1,−2,…, where it has poles. We then use the residue theorem of Lecture 19 in the opposite direction: instead of evaluating an integral by residues, we evaluate an infinite sum by writing its terms as residues and estimating an integral. The lecture reads in three stages: meromorphic functions and unique continuation (Section 21.1), the gamma function and its continuation (Sections 21.2–21.3), and residue sums (Section 21.4).

21.1 Meromorphic functions and unique continuation

Many functions of this course are analytic except at isolated poles: rational functions, tan⁡z,\tan ztanz, and the gamma function below. We give them a name.

Definition 21.1 (Meromorphic function). Let U⊂CU\subset\CU⊂C be open. A function fff is meromorphic on UUU if there is a set S⊂US\subset US⊂U with the following properties: each point z∈Uz\in Uz∈U has a disc Br(z)⊂UB_r(z)\subset UBr​(z)⊂U that contains no point of SSS other than possibly zzz itself; fff is analytic on U∖S;U\setminus SU∖S; and each point of SSS is a pole of f.ff.

The first property says that SSS has no limit point in UUU in the sense of Lecture 18: the poles do not accumulate at any point of U.UU. It also makes U∖SU\setminus SU∖S open: a point w∈U∖Sw\in U\setminus Sw∈U∖S has a disc Br(w)⊂UB_r(w)\subset UBr​(w)⊂U without points of SSS other than w,ww, and w∉S.w\notin Sw∈/S. By the first property, fff is analytic on a punctured disc about each point of S,SS, so every point of SSS is an isolated singular point of fff in the sense of Lecture 18.

A rational function P/Q,P/QP/Q, with the common zeros of PPP and QQQ cancelled, is meromorphic on C,\CC, with SSS the set of zeros of Q.QQ. The functions πcot⁡(πz)=πcos⁡(πz)/sin⁡(πz)\pi\cot(\pi z)=\pi\cos(\pi z)/\sin(\pi z)πcot(πz)=πcos(πz)/sin(πz) and π/sin⁡(πz)\pi/\sin(\pi z)π/sin(πz) are meromorphic on C\CC with S=Z.S=\ZS=Z. To see this, write z=x+iy.z=x+\iu yz=x+iy. The definitions of sin⁡\sinsin and cos⁡\coscos through e±iz\ee^{\pm\iu z}e±iz (Lecture 15) give sin⁡z=sin⁡xcosh⁡y+icos⁡xsinh⁡y,cos⁡z=cos⁡xcosh⁡y−isin⁡xsinh⁡y.\sin z=\sin x\cosh y+\iu\cos x\sinh y,\qquad \cos z=\cos x\cosh y-\iu\sin x\sinh y .sinz=sinxcoshy+icosxsinhy,cosz=cosxcoshy−isinxsinhy.(21.1) With cosh⁡2y=1+sinh⁡2y\cosh^2y=1+\sinh^2ycosh2y=1+sinh2y this yields ∣sin⁡z∣2=sin⁡2x+sinh⁡2y,∣cos⁡z∣2=cos⁡2x+sinh⁡2y,\abs{\sin z}^2=\sin^2x+\sinh^2y,\qquad \abs{\cos z}^2=\cos^2x+\sinh^2y ,∣sinz∣2=sin2x+sinh2y,∣cosz∣2=cos2x+sinh2y,(21.2) Hence sin⁡(πz)=0\sin(\pi z)=0sin(πz)=0 exactly when sinh⁡(πy)=0\sinh(\pi y)=0sinh(πy)=0 and sin⁡(πx)=0,\sin(\pi x)=0sin(πx)=0, that is, when zzz is an integer. Each integer nnn is a simple zero, because the derivative πcos⁡(πn)=π(−1)n\pi\cos(\pi n)=\pi(-1)^nπcos(πn)=π(−1)n is not 0.00. By Lecture 18 a quotient g/qg/qg/q with g(n)≠0g(n)\ne0g(n)=0 and a simple zero of qqq at nnn has a simple pole there.

The function e1/z\ee^{1/z}e1/z is not meromorphic on C,\CC, because its singularity at 000 is essential (Lecture 18). No function analytic on C∖{0}\C\setminus\{0\}C∖{0} is a logarithm of z,zz, by the proposition of Lecture 16 on the absence of a logarithm around the origin. The principal logarithm is analytic on its cut plane, but no function meromorphic near a point x<0x<0x<0 of the cut agrees with it off the cut. Such a function cannot have a pole at x,xx, because Log⁡\LogLog is bounded near x.xx. It cannot be analytic at x,xx, because the two boundary values of Log⁡\LogLog at xxx differ by 2πi2\pi\iu2πi (Lecture 16).

The identity theorem of Lecture 18 applies on a domain, a nonempty open set in which any two points are joined by a polygonal path in the set (Lecture 15). For a meromorphic function the relevant domain is U∖S,U\setminus SU∖S, and for the sets of poles in this lecture we check directly that it is a domain.

Lemma 21.2 (The plane minus a set of real points). Let S⊂RS\subset\RS⊂R be a set with S≠RS\ne\RS=R and without limit points in C.\CC. Then C∖S\C\setminus SC∖S is a domain.

Proof. The set C∖S\C\setminus SC∖S is open by the remark after Definition 21.1, applied with U=C.U=\CU=C. We join every point of C∖S\C\setminus SC∖S to i\iui by a polygonal path in C∖S.\C\setminus SC∖S. The upper half-plane Im⁡z>0\Im z>0Imz>0 is convex and contains no point of S,SS, so a point there is joined to i\iui by a segment. A real point x∉Sx\notin Sx∈/S is joined to x+ix+\iux+i by a vertical segment, which meets R\RR only at x.xx. For the lower half-plane choose x0∈R∖S.x_0\in\R\setminus Sx0​∈R∖S. A point zzz with Im⁡z<0\Im z<0Imz<0 is joined by a segment to x0−i,x_0-\iux0​−i, then vertically to x0+ix_0+\iux0​+i through x0,x_0x0​, and then to i.\iui. ■

The lemma applies to S=ZS=\ZS=Z and to S={0,−1,−2,…}.S=\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\}S={0,−1,−2,…}. A disc of radius 12\tfrac1221​ about an integer contains no other integer. A point z∉Zz\notin\Zz∈/Z has a nearest integer n,nn, and the disc Br(z)B_r(z)Br​(z) with r=∣z−n∣>0r=\abs{z-n}>0r=∣z−n∣>0 contains no integer.

Definition 21.3 (Meromorphic continuation). Let V⊂UV\subset UV⊂U be nonempty open sets, and let fff be analytic on V.VV. A meromorphic continuation of fff to UUU is a function FFF meromorphic on U,UU, with a set of poles S,SS, such that F=fF=fF=f on V∖S.V\setminus SV∖S.

Proposition 21.4 (Uniqueness of meromorphic continuation). Let UUU be a domain, and let S⊂US\subset US⊂U be a set without limit points in UUU such that U∖SU\setminus SU∖S is a domain. If two functions analytic on U∖SU\setminus SU∖S agree on a set that has a limit point in U∖S,U\setminus SU∖S, then they agree on U∖S.U\setminus SU∖S. In particular, a function analytic on a nonempty open set V⊂UV\subset UV⊂U has at most one meromorphic continuation to UUU whose poles lie in S.SS.

Proof. First, the difference of two such functions is analytic on the domain U∖S,U\setminus SU∖S, and its zeros have a limit point there. By the identity theorem of Lecture 18 the difference is 000 on U∖S.U\setminus SU∖S. Next, two meromorphic continuations of fff with poles in SSS are analytic on U∖SU\setminus SU∖S and agree on the nonempty open set V∖S,V\setminus SV∖S, every point of which is a limit point of it. By the first statement they agree on U∖S.U\setminus SU∖S. ■

Hence a meromorphic function on C\CC whose poles lie in a set SSS as in Lemma 21.2 is determined by its values on any segment or small disc outside S.SS.

Continuing a function that is already analytic on the plane minus a set of poles differs from continuing a logarithm along paths. Lecture 16 followed a branch of the logarithm along a path through a chain of discs. We now make this idea precise and prove the uniqueness announced there.

The proposition does not say that a continuation exists. Along a closed path the continuation need not return to its starting function. The next proposition shows that it does return for a function analytic on the plane minus a set of poles.

Proposition 21.7 (Continuation without a choice). Let SSS satisfy the hypotheses of Lemma 21.2, and let GGG be analytic on C∖S.\C\setminus SC∖S. Then every continuation along a path whose discs VjV_jVj​ lie in C∖S,\C\setminus SC∖S, and which starts with a function f1f_1f1​ equal to GGG near the initial point, ends with fN=Gon VN.f_N=G\quad\text{on }V_N .fN​=Gon VN​.

Proof. We argue by induction on j.jj. The disc V1V_1V1​ is a domain, and f1=Gf_1=Gf1​=G on a smaller disc, so f1=Gf_1=Gf1​=G on V1V_1V1​ by the identity theorem. If fj=Gf_j=Gfj​=G on Vj,V_jVj​, then fj+1=fj=Gf_{j+1}=f_j=Gfj+1​=fj​=G on Vj∩Vj+1,V_j\cap V_{j+1}Vj​∩Vj+1​, which is a nonempty open set, so fj+1=Gf_{j+1}=Gfj+1​=G on Vj+1V_{j+1}Vj+1​ by the identity theorem. ■

The conclusion holds whatever the path, closed or not. For the logarithm there is no such GGG on C∖{0}.\C\setminus\{0\}C∖{0}. Lecture 16 continued the logarithm along the upper and the lower half of the circle ∣z∣=4,\abs z=4∣z∣=4, and the two continuations arrived at −4-4−4 with values that differ by 2πi.2\pi\iu2πi. So choosing a branch of the logarithm means choosing a cut, and the value depends on that choice. The gamma function below is analytic on C\CC minus its poles, so its continuation involves no choice. Going around a pole changes nothing, and going around a branch point changes the value.

21.3 Continuation of the gamma function

The recurrence, read backwards as Γ(z)=Γ(z+1)/z,\Gamma(z)=\Gamma(z+1)/zΓ(z)=Γ(z+1)/z, expresses Γ\GammaΓ at zzz through its value at a point one unit to the right. Applied mmm times, it reaches the half-plane U0U_0U0​ from any point with Re⁡z>−m.\Re z>-mRez>−m. Let S={0,−1,−2,…},Um={z∈C:Re⁡z>−m}∖{0,−1,…,−m+1}(m≥1).S=\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\},\qquad U_m=\{z\in\C:\Re z>-m\}\setminus\{0,-1,\ldots,-m+1\}\quad(m\ge1).S={0,−1,−2,…},Um​={z∈C:Rez>−m}∖{0,−1,…,−m+1}(m≥1).

Theorem 21.10 (Continuation of the gamma function). There is a function analytic on C∖S\C\setminus SC∖S that equals Γ\GammaΓ on U0.U_0U0​. Written again as Γ,\GammaΓ, it satisfies Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z)(z∈C∖S),\Gamma(z+1)=z\Gamma(z)\qquad(z\in\C\setminus S),Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z)(z∈C∖S),(21.5) and each point −n-n−n with n=0,1,2,…n=0,1,2,\ldotsn=0,1,2,… is a simple pole with Res⁡z=−nΓ=(−1)nn!.\Res_{z=-n}\Gamma=\frac{(-1)^n}{n!} .Resz=−n​Γ=n!(−1)n​.(21.6) In particular, Γ\GammaΓ is meromorphic on C.\CC.

Proof. We construct the extension on each set Um,U_mUm​, check that the pieces agree, and then read off the recurrence and the poles.

No later result of this course depends on the following identity. It is an optional extension, and we cite it.

Theorem 21.12 (Reflection formula · cited). For every z∈C∖Z,z\in\C\setminus\Zz∈C∖Z, Γ(z)Γ(1−z)=πsin⁡(πz).\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z)=\frac\pi{\sin(\pi z)} .Γ(z)Γ(1−z)=sin(πz)π​.

The sibling course Real and Complex Analysis proves it in AN 13, in the section "Beta and reflection" (AN writes sss for our z),zz), and Beals and Wong prove it as Theorem 2.2.3. For 0<α<1,0<\alpha<10<α<1, AN 13 writes Γ(α)Γ(1−α)\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(1-\alpha)Γ(α)Γ(1−α) as the beta integral B(α,1−α),B(\alpha,1-\alpha)B(α,1−α), which the substitution t=x/(1+x)t=x/(1+x)t=x/(1+x) turns into the integral ∫0∞xα−1 ⁣dx/(1+x)=π/sin⁡(πα)\int_0^\infty x^{\alpha-1}\dd x/(1+x)=\pi/\sin(\pi\alpha)∫0∞​xα−1dx/(1+x)=π/sin(πα) of Lecture 20. The step to the beta integral changes variables in a double integral over the quarter-plane and exchanges the order of integration. Lecture 22 states the exchange for the improper integrals of this course as its Fubini–Tonelli rule I3, but its rules contain no change of variables for an improper double integral. So this step rests on AN 13, which justifies it by the Fubini–Tonelli theorem and the change-of-variables rule. AN 4 states both rules for Lebesgue integrals and cites them. The identity theorem then extends the formula to C∖Z.\C\setminus\ZC∖Z.

At z=12z=\tfrac12z=21​ the formula gives Γ(12)2=π.\Gamma(\tfrac12)^2=\piΓ(21​)2=π. It also shows that Γ\GammaΓ has no zeros off the integers, because its right side has none, and Γ(n)=(n−1)!≠0\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!\ne0Γ(n)=(n−1)!=0 at the positive integers.

21.4 Residue sums

The residue theorem turns an integral into a sum of residues. Read in the other direction, it turns a sum into an integral, which can then be estimated. To sum the values h(n)h(n)h(n) of a rational function hhh over the integers, we need an auxiliary function with a simple pole of residue 111 at every integer, so that the residue of the product at nnn is h(n).h(n)h(n). We also need it to stay bounded on a sequence of closed paths that enclose more and more integers.

The function πcot⁡(πz)\pi\cot(\pi z)πcot(πz) has both properties. Its poles are the integers, by Section 21.1, and Lecture 18 found its residue 111 at each of them. For an alternating sum we use π/sin⁡(πz).\pi/\sin(\pi z)π/sin(πz). For the paths we take squares whose sides cross the real and the imaginary axis halfway between two integers. Summary

A meromorphic function is analytic except at poles that do not accumulate in its domain. By the identity theorem, a meromorphic continuation to C\CC with its poles in a set of real points without accumulation is unique. A function already analytic on the plane minus such a set continues along every path that avoids the poles without a choice, and a logarithm does not. The gamma integral is analytic on the right half-plane by the lemma on parameter integrals, and the recurrence continues it to a meromorphic function on C.\CC. The function πcot⁡(πz)\pi\cot(\pi z)πcot(πz) has residue 111 at every integer and is bounded on the squares CN,C_NCN​, independently of N.NN. For a rational h=P/Qh=P/Qh=P/Q with deg⁡Q≥deg⁡P+2\deg Q\ge\deg P+2degQ≥degP+2 and no zero of QQQ at an integer, the residue theorem on CNC_NCN​ and the cutoff estimate turn ∑n∈Zh(n)\sum_{n\in\Z}h(n)∑n∈Z​h(n) into a finite sum of residues at the zeros of Q.QQ.

  • Continuation: two continuations along a path that start with the same function near its initial point end with the same function near its endpoint; a meromorphic function on C\CC whose poles lie on the real axis without accumulating is determined by its values near one point; if a function is analytic on all of C\CC minus such a set of poles, every continuation along a path that avoids these poles, starting from that function, ends with it; a branch of the logarithm needs an open set on which the argument is chosen continuously, and a cut is one way to obtain such a set.

  • Gamma: Γ(z)=∫0∞tz−1e−t ⁣dt\Gamma(z)=\int_0^\infty t^{z-1}\ee^{-t}\dd tΓ(z)=∫0∞​tz−1e−tdt is analytic for Re⁡z>0;\Re z>0Rez>0; Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z)\Gamma(z+1)=z\Gamma(z)Γ(z+1)=zΓ(z) continues it to C∖{0,−1,−2,…},\C\setminus\{0,-1,-2,\ldots\}C∖{0,−1,−2,…}, with Res⁡z=−nΓ=(−1)n/n!;\Res_{z=-n}\Gamma=(-1)^n/n!Resz=−n​Γ=(−1)n/n!; for Re⁡z≤0\Re z\le0Rez≤0 the integral does not converge absolutely, and for real z≤0z\le0z≤0 it diverges.

  • Residue sums: for a rational h=P/Qh=P/Qh=P/Q with deg⁡Q≥deg⁡P+2\deg Q\ge\deg P+2degQ≥degP+2 and no zero of QQQ at an integer, ∑n∈Zh(n)=−∑jRes⁡z=zj(πcot⁡(πz)h)\sum_{n\in\Z}h(n)=-\sum_j\Res_{z=z_j}(\pi\cot(\pi z)h)∑n∈Z​h(n)=−∑j​Resz=zj​​(πcot(πz)h) and ∑n∈Z(−1)nh(n)=−∑jRes⁡z=zj(πh/sin⁡(πz));\sum_{n\in\Z}(-1)^nh(n)=-\sum_j\Res_{z=z_j}(\pi h/\sin(\pi z))∑n∈Z​(−1)nh(n)=−∑j​Resz=zj​​(πh/sin(πz)); the proof uses ∣cot⁡(πz)∣≤coth⁡(π/2)\abs{\cot(\pi z)}\le\coth(\pi/2)∣cot(πz)∣≤coth(π/2) and ∣1/sin⁡(πz)∣≤1\abs{1/\sin(\pi z)}\le1∣1/sin(πz)∣≤1 on CN.C_NCN​.

Self-check

4 questions. Answer without looking back at the notes; a first miss gives a hint and a second try. Enter numbers with a decimal point.

1. Two single-valued meromorphic functions on the same connected open set agree on a nonempty open subset where both are analytic. What can happen elsewhere in the set?

Hint. Apply the identity theorem away from the poles, then compare the functions on punctured discs.

Removing the isolated poles leaves a connected open set, so the identity theorem gives equality there. Equality on each punctured disc fixes every Laurent coefficient, including each principal part. A single-valued meromorphic function returns to the same value after a loop avoiding its poles. Simple connectedness is unnecessary.

2. Use the recurrence of the gamma function to find Res⁡z=−3Γ(z)\Res_{z=-3}\Gamma(z)Resz=−3​Γ(z). Round to two decimal places.

Enter a valid number using a decimal point.

Hint. Shift the gamma argument until it reaches the right half-plane and isolate the vanishing factor.

Near −3-3−3 the recurrence gives Γ(z)=Γ(z+4)/[z(z+1)(z+2)(z+3)]\Gamma(z)=\Gamma(z+4)/[z(z+1)(z+2)(z+3)]Γ(z)=Γ(z+4)/[z(z+1)(z+2)(z+3)]. Multiply by z+3z+3z+3 and set z=−3z=-3z=−3. The numerator is Γ(1)=1\Gamma(1)=1Γ(1)=1 and the remaining product is (−3)(−2)(−1)=−6(-3)(-2)(-1)=-6(−3)(−2)(−1)=−6. The residue is −1/6-1/6−1/6.

3. Using the residue sum for h(z)=1/(z2+1)h(z)=1/(z^2+1)h(z)=1/(z2+1), what is the sum ∑n∈Zh(n)\sum_{n\in\Z}h(n)∑n∈Z​h(n)?

Hint. Choose the auxiliary function whose residue is one at every integer. Then find the residues at the two poles of hhh.

The auxiliary function is πcot⁡(πz)\pi\cot(\pi z)πcot(πz). At z=iz=\iuz=i the product with hhh has residue πcot⁡(πi)/(2i)=−πcoth⁡π/2\pi\cot(\pi\iu)/(2\iu)=-\pi\coth\pi/2πcot(πi)/(2i)=−πcothπ/2. The product is odd, so the residue at z=−iz=-\iuz=−i is the same. The square integrals tend to zero by quadratic decay, hence the integer sum is the negative of the two residues’ sum. Dropping that minus sign gives the negative answer. The cosecant kernel instead sums alternating terms. Subtracting one omits the term at zero.

4. For h(z)=1/(z+1/2)h(z)=1/(z+1/2)h(z)=1/(z+1/2), which obstacle prevents using the lecture’s cotangent residue-sum theorem as stated?

Hint. Compare the decay of hhh with the growth of the contour length.

The pole at −1/2-1/2−1/2 is simple and is not an integer. The cotangent remains bounded on the chosen squares. The decay O(1/∣z∣)O(1/\abs z)O(1/∣z∣) offsets the linear growth of the square’s length, leaving a bounded estimate that need not tend to zero. The absolute terms behave like 1/∣n∣1/\abs n1/∣n∣, so absolute convergence fails. A symmetric sum would need its own argument.
